overview.intro: The Mauryan Empire (c. 322-185 BCE) was the first pan-Indian empire, founded by Chandragupta Maurya with the guidance of his minister Kautilya (Chanakya) and brought to its moral height by Ashoka the Great. This chapter studies the four key sources - the Arthashastra, Megasthenes' Indika, the Ashokan Edicts and the Sanchi Stupa - the kings in chronological order, the machinery of Mauryan administration, and the principles and impact of Ashoka's Dhamma.

blocks.text: After Alexander's invasion (326 BCE) weakened the north-west, Chandragupta Maurya, aided by Kautilya, overthrew the Nanda dynasty of Magadha (c. 322 BCE) and built an empire from Afghanistan to Bengal. He defeated Seleucus Nicator c. 305 BCE, acquiring territories and a Greek ambassador, Megasthenes. His son Bindusara extended it south; his grandson Ashoka (r. c. 273/269-232 BCE) conquered Kalinga (c. 261 BCE) and, moved by its slaughter, adopted Dhamma-vijaya - conquest by righteousness - becoming history's most famous convert to ethical rule. The empire lasted till c. 185 BCE, when the last Maurya was displaced by Pushyamitra Sunga.

Sources. Arthashastra: Kautilya's Sanskrit treatise on kingship, spies, taxation and administration - the manual of Mauryan government. Indika: Megasthenes' description (preserved in later quotations) of Pataliputra, the seven castes of society, the absence of slavery in his view, and the lush fertility of the land. Ashokan Edicts: royal proclamations on rocks and pillars from Kandahar to Kalsi, written mostly in Prakrit (Brahmi script; Kharoshthi in the north-west; Greek-Aramaic at Kandahar) - the royal voice itself, on Dhamma, welfare and remorse. Sanchi Stupa: the Great Stupa begun by Ashoka over Buddha's relics, with its later gateways (toranas) - evidence of Mauryan foundations of Buddhist architecture and art.

Kings in chronological order. Chandragupta Maurya (c. 322-298 BCE): founder; with Kautilya overthrew the Nandas; defeated Seleucus; united north India; became a Jain and died by sallekhana at Shravanabelagola. Bindusara (c. 298-273 BCE): 'Amitraghata' (slayer of foes) to Greeks; extended the empire to Mysore; patronised the Ajivika sect. Ashoka (c. 273/269-232 BCE): after a succession struggle, ruled the greatest empire; Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) transformed him; adopted Dhamma, missionary Buddhism, edicts, welfare. Later kings: Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan and Brihadratha (last, murdered by his commander Pushyamitra Sunga, c. 185 BCE) - a rapid decline.

Administration - the king and centre. The king was the head of the government, army and justice; the Arthashastra made his day an itinerary of court, accounts and inspection. He was aided by a council of ministers (mantrins), the amatyas, and a trained bureaucracy: the sannidhata (treasurer), samaharta (collector of revenue), purohita (priest), senapati (army chief). Spies (gudhapurushas) in two streams (sanstha and sanchara) reported on officials and citizens; C2 (counter-intelligence) was a state art. Kautilya's state ran courts, mines, forests, textiles, mints - almost an industrial state.

Administration - provinces and cities. The empire was divided into provinces: four great viceroyalties at Taxila (north-west), Ujjain (west), Tosali (east) and Suvarnagiri (south), besides the metropolitan province of Pataliputra - princes (kumaras) usually governed them. Provinces split into districts (janapada) under pradeshikas, sub-districts under sthanikas, and villages under gramikas. Cities like Pataliputra had their own board of thirty officials in six committees looking after industry, foreigners, births-deaths, trade regulation, manufactured goods and sales tax - Megasthenes describes this municipal board.

Administration - revenue and army. Land revenue (bali/bhaga), custom duties, mines, forests, salt and spirits monopolies fed the treasury; the samaharta collected, the sannidhata stored. The army - six committees of thirty (per Megasthenes) for infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots, navy and transport - guarded a frontier like no earlier Indian state's. Roads: the Royal Highway (Uttarapatha) from Pataliputra to Taxila, and a southern trunk to the Deccan, with wells, rest-houses and mile-stones, knit the empire together.

Ashoka's Dhamma - principles. Dhamma was not a new religion but a moral code for society, rooted in the edicts: obedience to elders and teachers; respectful treatment of slaves, servants and the poor; liberality to Brahmanas and Sramanas; ahimsa - sparing animals (banned sacrifices, reduced royal kitchen slaughter, listed protected species) and abstaining from violence; religious tolerance among all sects; truthfulness, piety and self-control. Ashoka appointed Dhamma Mahamattas (c. 256 BCE) to teach it, sent missions abroad (son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka; missionaries to Syria, Egypt, Greece), built hospitals for men and animals, planted shade trees, dug wells, made rest houses, and personally toured (dhamma-yatas) to instruct.

Ashoka's Dhamma - impact. Within the empire, Dhamma softened the harsh edges of a coercive state - masters and servants, rich and poor were urged to humane conduct; animal sacrifice declined; welfare measures prefigured the modern welfare state. Abroad, Buddhist missions carried the faith to Sri Lanka and western Asia, making Buddhism a world religion and India its teacher. Ashoka's own image - Beloved-of-the-Gods (Devanampiya Piyadassi) - became the model of the righteous ruler; his lion capital of Sarnath is now India's national emblem and his wheel (chakra) on the national flag. But the edicts' very energy and the empire's post-Ashoka weakness also suggest the strain Dhamma's ethics placed on realpolitik; historians debate its role in Mauryan decline.

items: Chandragupta Maurya - Founder (c. 322 BCE); unifier of north India; defeated Seleucus; ended as a Jain ascetic at Shravanabelagola.
Kautilya (Chanakya) - Chandragupta's minister and author of the Arthashastra; architect of Mauryan statecraft.
Bindusara - Second emperor, called Amitraghata by Greeks; extended the empire southward.
Ashoka - Third emperor; Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) turned him to Dhamma; the edicts' author; the 'Ashoka the Great' of history.
Megasthenes - Seleucid ambassador at Pataliputra; wrote Indika describing Mauryan India.
Nanda unpopularity and Alexander's withdrawal created a power vacuum in Magadha and the north-west.
Kautilya's strategy and statecraft gave Chandragupta organisation and doctrine.
Magadha's resources - iron, elephants, fertile Ganga plains, rivers as highways.
Bindusara's and Ashoka's consolidations of frontier and south.
First political unification of most of the subcontinent under one government.
A professional bureaucracy, spy system and standardised administration as models for later ages.
Buddhism's rise to a world religion via royal missions and stupas.
Ashokan ethical statecraft entering Indian political memory (emblem, chakra today).
Empire's fall (c. 185 BCE) after Brihadratha's murder - Sunga dynasty follows.

blocks.text: Dhamma-vijaya vs digvijaya: Conquest by righteousness after Kalinga versus the old conquest by arms.
Arthashastra vs Indika: Internal manual of statecraft in Sanskrit versus a Greek outsider's description of the empire.
Rock edicts vs Pillar edicts: Edicts cut on natural rock faces versus engraved on free-standing polished sandstone pillars.
Sannidhata vs Samaharta: Head of the treasury and stores versus chief revenue collector.

items: Writing Bindusara as 'Bindusar' or as Ashoka's son - he was Chandragupta's son, Ashoka's father.
Claiming the Arthashastra was written by Ashoka - it is Kautilya's.
Saying Megasthenes was Chandragupta's ambassador to Greece - he was the Greek ambassador in India.
Confusing Dhamma with Buddhism itself - Dhamma was a broader moral code, though Ashoka was a Buddhist.
Saying the Mauryan army had no navy - Megasthenes lists a committee for the navy.
Mixing up province capitals (Taxila/Ujjain/Tosali/Suvarnagiri) with edict sites.

questions.prompt: Which Mauryan ruler's court did Megasthenes attend?
questions.explanation: He was Seleucus's ambassador and wrote the Indika.

questions.answer: Conquest by righteousness/moral suasion instead of arms - Ashoka's ideal after Kalinga.
questions.explanation: Contrast with digvijaya, conquest of the quarters by force.

questions.prompt: Name the four provinces of the Mauryan Empire with their capitals.
questions.explanation: Usually governed by princes (kumaras); Pataliputra was the imperial capital.
questions.commonMistake: Listing edict sites instead of provincial capitals.

questions.prompt: Mention any two principles of Ashoka's Dhamma.
questions.answer: Any two of: obedience and respect to elders, teachers and priests; humane treatment of slaves, servants and the poor; liberality to Brahmanas and Sramanas; ahimsa - non-injury to animals and men; religious tolerance towards all sects; truthfulness, piety and self-control.
questions.explanation: Dhamma was a social-moral code, not a new religion.
questions.commonMistake: Describing Dhamma as Buddhist conversion alone.

questions.prompt: What information do the Ashokan edicts provide?
questions.answer: They record Ashoka's Dhamma and its principles, his remorse after Kalinga, welfare measures (wells, trees, rest houses, medical care for men and animals), instructions to officials, and religious tolerance - written in Prakrit on rocks and pillars across the empire.
questions.explanation: The edicts are the emperor's own voice - primary evidence of his policy.

questions.prompt: How did the Kalinga war change Ashoka's policy? Explain.
questions.answer: Though victorious, Ashoka was moved by the slaughter - 'a hundred and fifty thousand deported, a hundred thousand slain' as the 13th Rock Edict records. He renounced war (bheri-ghosha replaced by dhamma-ghosha), embraced Dhamma as state policy, banned animal sacrifice and regulated the royal kitchen's slaughter, appointed Dhamma Mahamattas, sent missions abroad (including Mahendra and Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka), and undertook welfare works - wells, trees, rest houses, hospitals for men and beasts. Conquest by arms gave way to conquest by righteousness.
questions.explanation: Link the war's horror to each policy change.
questions.commonMistake: Saying he became a monk or abandoned the empire.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Arthashastra and the Indika as sources of Mauryan history.
questions.answer: The Arthashastra, attributed to Kautilya, is an internal Sanskrit treatise on statecraft - kingship, spies, taxation, departments - telling us how the state was meant to run. The Indika, by the Greek ambassador Megasthenes, is an outsider's description of what he saw at Pataliputra - the city's administration, the seven divisions of society, the fertility of the land. One is a manual (prescriptive), the other an eyewitness account (descriptive); used together with the edicts, they cross-verify Mauryan administration.
questions.explanation: Authorship, language, nature (manual vs account) and use.

questions.prompt: Describe the central administration of the Mauryan Empire.
questions.answer: At the head stood the king, in whom all executive, legislative and military power was vested; the Arthashastra schedules his day of court and inspection. He was advised by the mantriparishad (council of ministers) and served by high officials: the mantrins, the purohita (priest-adviser), the samaharta (chief collector of revenue), the sannidhata (keeper of the treasury and stores), the senapati (commander) and the nyayakas/judges. A vast bureaucracy of amatyas ran departments of revenue, mines, forests, textiles, mints, passports and trade; spies (gudhapurushas) in two streams reported on officials and the people. The empire was divided into provinces (four great viceroyalties - Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali, Suvarnagiri - usually under kumaras), districts under pradeshikas and sthanikas, and villages under gramikas with village elders. Cities like Pataliputra had a municipal board of thirty members in six committees (per Megasthenes) for industry, foreigners, births/deaths, trade, manufactures and sales-tax. The army, under six committees (infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots, navy, transport), was permanent and paid in cash; land revenue (bhaga, often 1/4 to 1/6 of produce) and trade taxes fed the treasury, while the Royal Highway linked provinces to the capital.
questions.explanation: King, ministers, departments, spies, provinces, city board, army, revenue.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only the provinces without the centre.

questions.prompt: Arrange the Mauryan rulers in chronological order: Bindusara, Brihadratha, Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka.
questions.answer: Chandragupta Maurya (c. 322-298 BCE) -> Bindusara (c. 298-273 BCE) -> Ashoka (c. 273/269-232 BCE) -> ... -> Brihadratha (last, c. 185 BCE).
questions.explanation: Founder, son, grandson, then the last of the line.
